4457.prule: No word-stress rule. Nyamwezi is a two-tone (H/L) language with high-tone shift (Schadeberg 1991; Kanijo 2019). Dahl 1904, the only source with an explicit 'accent' statement, first gives the positions of the pitch Hochton ('Die eigentlichen Töne', pp. 106-120) and then says the dynamic Haupt- and Nebenakzent 'can be found on any syllable' (ultima to 6th-last); the most frequent placement is main accent on the penult and secondary on the ultima (so the prefix takes the main accent with a monosyllabic stem), followed by six further listed combinations. No computable position is stated; the accent is not shown to be independent of tone.
4457.srule: Dahl 1904: every word with a main accent also carries one secondary accent (Nebenakzent); monosyllables carry neither. The secondary may fall on any syllable from the ultima to the fifth-from-last. Most often it is on the ultima with the main accent on the penult (disyllabic words/stems; with a monosyllabic word-final stem the prefix has the main accent and the stem the secondary). Other common combinations (p. 122, groups I-VI): main antepenult + secondary ultima; main antepenult + secondary penult; secondary antepenult + main penult; main fourth-from-last + secondary penult (full reduplications); further combinations and 5th/6th-last placements pp. 125-126. No alternating rhythm is described.

4461.prule: No word-stress rule. Runyankore/Nkore-Kiga is a tone language (H, L, falling; falling only on a long utterance/phrase-penultimate syllable; final H retracts to the penult phrase-finally) and, per Easterday 2019 on the authority of Taylor 1985: 202-205, 'does not have word stress'. Johnson 1976 (SCOPIL 3, pp. 209-215) reports a sociolectal split: 'High Runyankore' keeps tone (most H and F tones on the penult), while 'Low Runyankore' has replaced H/F tone with a penultimate stress-accent; this Low variety is the entry 'Runyankore, Low (Uganda) penult' in the printed Goedemans & van der Hulst 2010 survey. No first-hand stress rule for the standard tonal variety is stated in any reachable source.

4462.dloc: §5 'Pitch-accent and Stress', p. 16 (fn. 12 on the same page); §3b 'Vowel Quantity', p. 10.
4462.prule: Weak, non-contrastive stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the word, independent of pitch and blind to syllable weight (every syllable is open, §4; vowel quantity is positional — penult lengthening, coalescence, elision — and the single quantity-only pair Watkins reports, nidá·dza 'I came and am now here' / nidá:dza 'I came, but did not remain', is an aspect distinction that 'may, of course, be employed with any verb', §3b, so there is no lexical length contrast to condition stress); the stress is decidedly strong only where the penult also carries the high tone, so stress and pitch-accent fuse there. Separately, the penult vowel is lengthened when the word stands alone or is the last word of a sound group (§3b).

4463.dq: All word-level pitch processes in Nyang’i can be accounted for with reference to two tone levels: high and low.
4463.prule: No stress rule. Beer 2017 (pp. 40-42) describes Nyang'i word prosody as lexically specified but non-contrastive pitch, handled with tone formalisms: the pitch features of a root are not predictable from segmental or prosodic context or from position in the word, are consistent across utterances, and are never the sole means of contrast; duration and amplitude do not track pitch, so 'the prosodic system is not more meaningfully described as a stress system than as a tone system'. Surface tones H, L, F (F only in a closed final syllable), two underlying tones; 'High tone and low tone may occur at any position in a word'.
4463.srule: Not mentioned in Beer 2017, sections 2.5-2.5.2 'Tone', pp. 40-48 (no stress system is described: word prosody is lexically specified, non-contrastive H/L pitch, 'High tone and low tone may occur at any position in a word'; secondary or rhythmic stress is not discussed).

4463.tone: Beer 2017 pp. 40-42: pitch is lexically specified per root but non-contrastive ('I have not identified any two words in Nyang’i that differ in meaning solely on the basis of pitch'). 'Is Nyang’i, then, a tone language? If Yip (2002:1)’s definition “A language is a ‘tone language’ if the pitch of the word can change the meaning of the word” is the standard by which a language is deemed a tone language, then Nyang’i is not a tone language.' By Hyman's (2001) lexical-specification definition it is included; 'Nyang’i lands between the two definitions'; 'I leave the question of whether or not Nyang’i is “a tone language” to the reader.' p. 42: 'The tones associated with a root are not predictable on the basis of segmental or prosodic context.' p. 52: 'Nyang’i is the only language of the three, then, that lacks contrastive pitch features. It retains, however, replacive tone phenomena in affixation.' On 'stress': the word occurs only in the acoustic-correlate sentence quoted, in Beer's summary of the earlier description (p. 4: Heine 1974/5 records 'four phonetic pitches and notation for primary stress'), and in a remark about Soo (p. 52: 'tone (or at least stress) may be grammatically contrastive... in Soo', with stress marks in the Soo example 2.14, not Nyang'i). So the Proto-Kuliak 'primary stress in any position' that Wikipedia carries from Heine 1976 is a 1970s notation over lexically given pitch, consistent with Beer's lexically specified tone rather than a synchronic stress…

4465.heavy: Heavy = the 'major foot': CVV, CVʔV, CVCrVr or CVrCrV (Vr, Cr = reduced vowel/consonant; a reduced segment 'receives less stress, is of shorter duration and is less clearly articulated', fn. 2). The unit is the foot, not the syllable: major feet are historically two CV syllables fused by reduction (kɔ+lɔ > kɔli) and are longer than one minor foot but shorter than two. Light = the CV minor foot. In syllable terms this approximates CVV (long vowel/diphthong) plus CVC-like fused disyllables (the reduced vowel of CVCrVr may go unarticulated, [kɔlʲ˺]); no existing value fits exactly, hence 'onset-or-other'.
4465.dflt: Initial foot: 'In such words, the primary stress falls on the initial foot.' (p. 3)
4465.prule: Word prominence ('stress', non-contrastive, cued by duration and articulation) goes to the word's major foot, i.e. the heavy foot of shape CVV, CVʔV, CVCrVr or CVrCrV (e.g. /kabiɛlɛ/ 'finger' = minor ka + major biɛ + minor lɛ, stress on biɛ; /kɔli/ 'hand' one CVCrVr major foot); light CV minor feet are unstressed and 'usually' the single major foot carries the greatest stress; most words have exactly one major foot; in words composed solely of minor feet the primary stress falls on the initial foot (/pe/, /tɔgɔ/, /cogolo/).

The first syllable of a phonological word is accorded stress. [p. 100] ... Another problem is that stress patterns of isolated words do not always agree with th…

4466.heavy: 'I define a syllable as strong if it either consist of more than two morae, or is the initial syllable of a word. Weak syllables, by contrast, are in non-initial position, and consist of at most two morae.' (p. 99; fn. 21: C(C), V and vowel length each weigh 0.5, summed and rounded to the nearest integer, halves up). By the letter of fn. 21 a closed short-vowel syllable is 2 morae, i.e. not 'more than two'; in the examples the effective contrast is nonetheless CV (weak) vs closed or long-vowelled syllables (CVC, CVCC, CVV: 'heavier', 'strong'), which take the non-initial stresses and, in the exceptional words, attract stress away from a light initial syllable. Weight conditions only the non-initial stresses and the exceptions, never the regular initial stress.
4466.prule: Regular pattern: the first syllable of every phonological word is stressed, regardless of syllable count, of whether the word begins with a vowel or a consonant, and of the weight of the initial syllable (the initial syllable counts as 'strong' by definition). Stress is non-contrastive and delimitative. Degrees of stress cannot be distinguished in the data, so all stressed syllables are marked alike; the initial stress is the invariant, quantity-insensitive component.
4466.srule: Further stresses (the source cannot distinguish degrees; all stresses are marked alike) fall on odd-numbered syllables counted from the initial: a non-final odd syllable (3rd, 5th) is stressed, a word-final odd syllable only if strong (more than two morae: closed or long-vowelled), so 'ba.ba.rli but 'ka.rriny.'kam, 'ku.rru.'lu.kun, 'wi.da.'ma.nga.'ran; in four-syllable roots a strong final may be stressed instead of a weak third ('ka.ja.na.'ngurr). Verb forms show a preference for the same stressed-unstressed alternation.
4466.quote: As in most Australian languages, stress is not phonemic in Nyulnyul: it does not serve a contrastive function, and no words are distinguished by different loci of stress. 4470.dq: Phrase stress is realized over stress groups, which are usually smaller than pause groups (although the two may coincide over one single phrase). One phrase stress is assigned to each stress group in a given utterance.
4470.dloc: p. 5 (section 1 'Phrase stress in Obolo'); page = scan page + 2.
4470.prule: Phrase-level stress only. One phrase stress per syntactically defined stress group (a verb phrase with its subject, objects and modifiers; each serial verb and each indirect object a separate group; a place/time/manner complement; a detached or coordinated noun phrase), cued by extra-high F0, high amplitude and extra length (stressed vowels 215-245 ms vs 118-181 ms unstressed, table p. 5). Which syllable of the group carries it is not fixed by position in the word: it gravitates to underlyingly non-low syllables and group boundaries (phonological), to extra-high-toned verbal prefixes, the first morpheme of a place/time/manner complement, extra-high verb roots and prominent subject NPs (morphosyntactic), and follows verb focus (semantic-pragmatic); certain extra-high grammatical morphemes (negative ka, future ma/mo/me, 3sg completive i, question words, interjections, imperatives) are automatically stressed. No word-level stress position is stated anywhere.
4470.srule: Not mentioned in Faraclas 1984 (JWAL 14(1): 3-17, whole article read): stress is phrasal only, one phrase stress per syntactically defined stress group; no word-level primary or secondary stress is described (p. 11 says only that pitch may be raised on syllables adjacent to the phrase-stressed syllable and that the stress sometimes spreads evenly over two or three syllables).

4470.tone: Obolo has three tonemes (high, low, extra high; earlier analyses had five, p. 3). Nouns: one lexical tone per syllable; verb stems: a single H or L distributed over the stem (p. 4). Extra high is both a lexical toneme and the main cue of phrase stress (p. 4); under phrase stress level tones become glides (extra high > fall to high, high > fall to low, low > rise to high). Extra high never occurs on verb stems (p. 13) and occurs on noun stems 'in cases where there is no apparent reason to postulate accent or stress at any level' (p. 13, scan with edge-clipped letters). 4482.cfw: Bloch (1914) argues at length that no word accent can be proven for Old Marathi and explains its vowel changes by a purely quantitative rhythm, while Tulpule (1960) only assumes an accented initial syllable in passing to account for vowel preservation, so an undetermined verdict is the safe reading until Master's (1964) grammar can be consulted.
